questions.title: When does prior possession of a firearm qualify as 'intrinsic' evidence rather than propensity evidence under Rule 404(b)?
questions.question_body: I'm reading the 8th Circuit opinion here regarding *United States v. Cutbank*. The district court allowed testimony that the victim had seen the defendant with the sawed-off rifle prior to the incident. The opinion distinguishes this as 'intrinsic evidence' relevant to 'establish ownership' rather than improper propensity character evidence. Could someone explain what makes something 'intrinsic' in a felon-in-possession case? How do we determine the line between proving ownership versus just suggesting a bad character?

questions.title: Can a Confrontation Clause challenge be cured by a jury instruction given at the close of trial?
questions.question_body: On page 6 of the opinion, the court suggests that a district court 'need not instruct the jury regarding each item of evidence at the time the evidence is admitted' if they provide an instruction 'at the close of trial.' I thought the Confrontation Clause requires the defendant to have the opportunity to cross-examine the declarant *at the time of the statement* or right away. The opinion cites *United States v. Charboneau* saying the declarant must actually appear in court, but doesn't explain delaying the instruction. Is there a specific nuance I'm missing about when the Confrontation Clause violation occurs?

questions.title: What is the legal nexus required for a USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) enhancement when charged with ACCA felonies?
questions.question_body: The defendant was found guilty of being a felon in possession AND had three prior violent felonies (triggering ACCA). The PSR applied a 4-level enhancement for 'possession in connection with another felony.' The opinion says the Guidelines would have produced a higher level (35) than just the ACCA level (34), but the 4B1.4(b) rule says the greater level applies. I'm confused how the enhancement under § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) interacts mathematically with the ACCA sentencing enhancements found by the jury. Does the 'another felony' in § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) mean the felony used as perjury on another charge, or the possession itself?

questions.title: Why does the court presume the district court considered § 3553(a) factors even if they aren't explicitly recited in the record?
questions.question_body: Under the 8th Circuit's reasoning, the court states 'we therefore presume that the district court considered and rejected' the arguments because the defendant argued them at sentencing. However, *Gall* says 'Before a court of appeals can consider the substantive reasonableness of a sentence, it must first ensure that the district court committed no significant procedural error.' If the judge just didn't write the words 'I considered this', is that enough to say the appellate court won't check for 'procedural error'? What is the standard if the judge mentions it but doesn't explain *why* the specific factors weight the sentence up, but not by a 'greater than necessary' amount?

questions.title: What is the actual standard for finding 'substantial prejudice' regarding cumulative evidentiary error?
questions.question_body: The court dismisses the appeal on the ground that any evidentiary errors were harmless. It quotes *DeMarce* and says we reverse only if the jury was 'substantially swayed.' But the opinion mentions 'cumulative effect of trial errors.' Is there a specific set of questions the appellate court asks before deciding the 'cumulative effect' was so minor that prejudice was absent? If I have dozens of technical R. Evid. errors and the evidence against the defendant is strong, does the court simply stack them and say 'it doesn't matter,' or does each error need to matter individually to proceed?

questions.title: Why does the police report require authentication before a witness can be cross-examined on its contents?
questions.question_body: The defendant tried to impeach a witness (C.F.) about statements she made to a police investigator. The court allowed questioning about what she said but sustained an objection when counsel tried to read the report into the record because it 'was not authored by [the witness].' The opinion says extrinsic evidence 'must still be authenticated.' I understand hearsay rules, but I thought if we are just using a report to make a witness lie, we don't need to authenticate the *report* itself, just establish the witness's perception. Why is the authentication requirement violated if the officer didn't testify or sign off on the report?
